subject: announcement
notes: The payload of an announcement, types/DhtAnnouncement.json: which bytes are an announcement and what they say, whether one is current enough to store, and the delegation a legacy node -- whose node key is its community key -- signs for itself.
A payload vector is wrong in at most one way, and what is contracted is what a caller can observe: whether the payload is taken, and the values that come out. Why one was refused is not.
`payload` is the authority. `text` is the same bytes for a reader, where they are text at all; a runner that uses it checks that it encodes to `payload`.

Every self-delegation was signed by libp2p-ffi itself (lp2p_delegation_sign, v0.1.2), its communityKey computed by lp2p_key_from_seed, and the result accepted by lp2p_delegation_verify: the vectors say what the network accepts. ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so a delegation is an exact value.
The frame around a payload -- version byte, delegation, payload -- is libp2p-ffi's and has no vector here.

The TypeScript runner is packages/contract-tests/src/announcement.test.ts. The C runner, fast-servers/tests/contract/test_announcement_contract.cpp, does not exist yet: the fast path parses no payload so far, and may lag behind the reference path. No regenerator: the values came from the oracle named above or are written out by hand.

id.note: Stable forever. A failure names this.

why.note: What this vector is load bearing for.

kind.note: payload, current or self-delegation: which of the three a vector tests, and so which of the fields below it carries.

text.note: payload: the bytes as text, for a reader. Null where they are not valid UTF-8 worth showing.

payload.note: payload: what arrived after the frame's version byte and delegation.

lastTaken.note: current: the announcedAt last stored for that community, null for none since the node started.

communitySeed.note: self-delegation: the community's 32-byte ed25519 seed, which is the node's too.

expect.accepted.note: payload: whether anything of it may be stored. The contract.

expect.api.note: payload: in the order sent; null when refused.

expect.stored.note: current: whether the announcement is stored.

expect.communityKey.note: self-delegation: the public key, node key and community key at once.

vectors.why: The ordinary case: a community with a URL that serves two API versions.
A single version is a list of one.
A community without a URL: it exists, and offers no federation API over HTTP.
How the format grows: a member this version does not know is ignored, not refused.
No member order and no whitespace rule: the payload is parsed, never compared.
DHT_ANNOUNCE_MAX_APIS entries are allowed.
A url of DHT_ANNOUNCE_URL_MAX_BYTES bytes fills the column and is allowed.
An api of DHT_ANNOUNCE_API_MAX_BYTES bytes fills the column and is allowed: letters, digits and underscores.
http is allowed beside https: a community may sit behind a proxy that ends TLS elsewhere, and development has no certificate.
A port between 1 and 65535.
A host alone. The federation client makes the URL end in a slash.
A dotted IPv4 address is a host of numeric labels.
A name without a dot. Whether a host is one this server should call is not the format's question.
%XX in a path segment, with hex digits of either case.
A member named twice. JSON.parse would keep the last and the C path's reader the first, so they would store two different URLs; neither wins, and the announcement is refused.
Zero is a number written without leading zeros. Whether it is current is the other kind of vector.
The largest instant the type holds.
DHT_ANNOUNCE_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES bytes exactly, padded with whitespace, are allowed.
One byte more than DHT_ANNOUNCE_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES, and otherwise valid.
No bytes are not JSON.
Bytes that are not JSON.
Legacy's hyperswarm shape, an array of { api, url } pairs, is not this format.
url is required, also for a community without one: it is then empty.
api is required.
announcedAt is required: without it an old announcement could be played back.
A member of another type refuses the announcement.
A single version is still a list.
Every entry of api is a string.
One entry more than DHT_ANNOUNCE_MAX_APIS, as legacy refuses it.
An api version has at least one byte.
One byte more than the column holds.
A version listed twice would be two rows under one unique key.
One byte more than the column holds.
Versions with nowhere to call them.
A URL that serves no version.
A JSON number loses precision in one parser and not in the other; an instant is a decimal string.
One instant has one spelling.
Digits only: no sign.
One more than the type holds.
No digits are not a number.
A byte of 0x80 or above anywhere refuses the announcement, as legacy refuses it: here the two bytes of a u-umlaut in the host.
The same character behind a JSON escape: every byte is ASCII and the string that comes out is not. Its length would be one in JavaScript and two in C.
A space is not in the alphabet of a path.
The rule holds for every member, not only for the ones this version reads: a reader must not have to know a member to notice it twice.
A member name spelled with an escape. Decoded it could be a second `url` that only one of the two readers recognises, so no name carries one.
Only http and https are called.
A scheme that names something on the receiving server itself.
One URL has one spelling: the scheme is lowercase.
One URL has one spelling: the host is lowercase.
A user and password before the host: what is shown and what is called then differ, the oldest trick there is.
No query: the client appends a path to the URL, and after a `?` that path would be an argument.
No fragment: everything the client appends after a `#` would never be sent.
Port 0 is not a port.
One more than the largest port.
One port has one spelling.
A colon with nothing after it.
A scheme and a path with nothing between them.
A label neither starts nor ends with a hyphen.
The root label written out is another spelling of the same name; there is one.
An underscore is not in the alphabet of a host name.
No IPv6 literal for now: a bracketed address is a second grammar to hold two parsers to, and no community is announced by one.
No `..` segment: what the URL says and what the server resolves it to then differ.
No `.` segment, for the same reason.
A backslash is read as a slash by some clients and not by others.
A percent sign is followed by two hex digits.
A host and a path alone are not a URL.
An api version is appended to the URL by the client, so it is letters, digits and underscores: nothing that is a path of its own.
The first announcement of a community since this node started, made just now.
Made DHT_ANNOUNCE_MAX_CLOCK_DIFFERENCE_SECONDS before the receiver's clock: still stored.
One millisecond older than that. This is the bound on playing an announcement back to a node that has just started.
A sender whose clock runs ahead by the limit: still stored.
One millisecond further ahead. Taken, it would shut out every honest announcement until the receiver's clock caught up.
The ordinary repeat: thirty seconds after the last one taken.
The same announcement again: not later, so not stored.
An older announcement played back within the clock limit, after a newer one was taken.
What a legacy node carries in every frame: its node key is its community key, so the delegation names one key twice and is signed by it.
The same with an expiry, which is part of what is signed.
